BIOCAL3D · RESULTS REVIEW · 15 OCTOBER 2026

Colour is highly predictive. The contribution of geometry is still unresolved.

All 23 reference experiments completed. PointNeXt-S with geometry and RGB achieved 63/64 correct validation classifications (98.6% balanced accuracy). Geometry-only baselines were substantially weaker. The next experiments should isolate colour shortcuts and scanner/reconstruction effects before choosing a fusion architecture.

Scope: these are baseline / partial / clean stage classifications, not annotated biofilm segmentation. Results use one checkpoint-selection validation set of six physical specimens. No held-out test, outer cross-validation or unseen-scanner assessment is present in this archive.

1 · The run and split audit passed

  • 512 scans, 48 physical specimens, G1–G6 and four scanners; no missing/unexpected/excluded scans in the exported audit.
  • 384 scans / 36 specimens in training; 64 / 6 in validation; 64 / 6 reserved for test. Each physical specimen belongs to exactly one partition across scanners and stages.
  • All 23 status files report complete; failures.json is empty. All 23 validation prediction files cover the same 64 scan IDs; labels, specimen/scanner identities, probability sums, predicted classes and confusion matrices were independently checked.
  • No duplicate geometry hashes in the full manifest. This checks exported identities/hashes; the raw meshes and checkpoints were not supplied for inference reruns.
  • Validation support is 24 baseline, 16 partial and 24 clean scans, arising from six baseline/clean specimens and four partial specimens. Four scanners of one specimen are correlated observations.
  • The archived runner/backend source hashes match the local delivered implementation used for this methodological review.

2 · Geometry alone: Sonata is the strongest of the repeated baseline settings

model mode seeds BA_mean BA_seed_SD partial_recall_mean
Sonata Frozen pretrained 3 59.49 2.89 56.25
TSGCNet Trained from scratch 3 51.39 7.35 12.50
Concerto Frozen pretrained 3 47.69 3.13 29.17
PointNeXt-S Trained from scratch 3 41.44 7.09 31.25

Chance balanced accuracy for three classes is 33.3%. Sonata has the best mean and the most balanced class recall in this repeated baseline comparison. TSGCNet’s partial recall averages only 12.5%; seeds 43 and 44 classify none of the partial scans correctly. PointNeXt-S seed 44 predicts baseline for every validation scan. A single overall score would conceal these failure modes.

These settings are not an architecture-only comparison: Sonata and Concerto use frozen pretrained encoders, while PointNeXt-S and TSGCNet are trained from scratch. TSGCNet also uses native triangle-centre features; equal point counts do not give equal underlying mesh resolution. Weak geometry-only results do not prove that biological surface geometry is uninformative.

3 · RGB is the largest observed improvement, with a bundled colour pathway

model variant BA accuracy partial_recall best_epoch
Concerto area_geometry 47.92 51.56 18.75 25
Concerto geometry_rgb 93.06 92.19 100.00 18
PointNeXt-S area_geometry 46.53 51.56 6.25 14
PointNeXt-S geometry_rgb 98.61 98.44 100.00 26

PointNeXt-S increases from 46.5% to 98.6% balanced accuracy (+52.1 percentage points); Concerto increases from 47.9% to 93.1% (+45.1 points). Both RGB runs correctly classify all 16 partial validation scans, but these represent four independent physical specimens. The only PointNeXt-S RGB error is TRIOS5 BCG2T0-1, baseline predicted partial (69.9% confidence).

Important implementation detail: the RGB runs both feed per-point RGB to the encoder and concatenate six pooled colour statistics (three mean and three maximum values) directly to the classifier head. This direct head path is confirmed by the matching runner source. The results establish that the combined RGB configuration is strong; they do not establish how much comes from spatial colour–geometry learning versus a global colour summary.

The existing colour-only logistic regression uses surface-area-weighted RGB means and standard deviations and reaches 77.8% balanced accuracy. It is useful evidence of a global colour signal, but it does not match the RGB head’s feature statistics or nonlinear classifier capacity. Therefore, subtracting 77.8% from 98.6% does not isolate a geometric contribution.

A decisive matched study would compare: (a) the same classifier on the exact six pooled colour values; (b) encoder features without the direct six-value pathway; (c) the current combined pathway; and (d) RGB permuted among positions within each scan, retaining its colour distribution. Train and evaluate matched permutation variants to distinguish loss of spatial information from a test-only distribution shift. Repeat the key variants across seeds and specimen folds. Include a mature-only (G3–G6) training comparison because partial stage is absent from G1–G2.

4 · Mesh reconstruction carries substantial stage information

control balanced_accuracy accuracy
scanner_only 33.33 37.50
face_count_only 33.33 37.50
scanner_face_count 72.92 78.12
roughness_geometry 48.61 51.56
colour_only 77.78 79.69

Scanner identity alone and face count alone each obtain 33.3% balanced accuracy, but their combination reaches 72.9%. That combination outperforms every repeated geometry-only baseline and is slightly above the single Concerto face-centre run (72.2%). It is not evidence that a neural model necessarily used face count, but it demonstrates a strong nuisance route available in these data.

New paired check: baseline has more triangles than clean in all 168 development scanner–specimen pairs (42 physical specimens × four scanners). Median paired baseline/clean triangle-count ratios are 1.85 for LABscanner, 1.48 for TRIOS3, 1.72 for TRIOS5 and 1.47 for iTERO. These are descriptive repeated observations, not 168 independent biological samples.

This could reflect real changes in reconstructed surface complexity, scanner reconstruction behaviour, export/decimation or acquisition conditions. The present data cannot distinguish those explanations. Equalizing the number of sampled points does not equalize the original triangulation, normals or retained geometric detail.

Next controls: preserve and compare original exports; record any decimation settings; sample by surface area; remesh to common physical resolution; repeat with an interior ROI to suppress crop-edge cues; and compare the same stage changes on a stable reference/phantom. If performance collapses after reconstruction and edge controls, the earlier score was not a robust measure of local biofilm topography.

5 · Sampling and scanner dependence limit the current ranking

Concerto changes from 47.9% balanced accuracy with area sampling to 72.2% with face centres (+24.3 points). PointNeXt-S changes from 46.5% to 44.4%. Removing normals reduces seed-42 balanced accuracy by about 10.4 points in both PointNeXt-S and Concerto, suggesting that the tested encoders use more than XYZ alone; that signal may still include reconstruction effects. Plane alignment gives only +0.7 points for PointNeXt-S and +6.3 points for Concerto; voxel averaging gives −4.2 and +3.5 points respectively. These are one-seed comparisons, so they require repetition before selecting a preprocessing strategy.

The face-centre QC shows median unique positions of 636 for TRIOS3 and 619 for TRIOS5, versus 2,048 for LABscanner and iTERO, despite 2,048 entries in every input. Duplicated samples and the scanner’s original reconstruction therefore remain relevant. Area sampling has 2,048 unique positions but interpolates the same low-resolution source surfaces; it cannot restore missing detail.

scanner model LABscanner TRIOS3 TRIOS5 iTERO
Concerto 79.63 33.33 35.19 42.59
PointNeXt-S 54.63 35.19 35.19 40.74
Sonata 86.11 54.63 47.22 50.00
TSGCNet 61.11 50.00 52.78 41.67

Values above are mean validation balanced accuracy across the three baseline seeds. Sonata is 86.1% on LABscanner but about 47–55% on the other scanners. Concerto shows an even larger LABscanner advantage. This supports testing scanner-specific reconstruction quality and transferability; it does not prove that resolution alone caused the differences.

PointNeXt-S RGB has 100% balanced accuracy on LABscanner, TRIOS3 and iTERO, and 94.4% on TRIOS5. Those scanners were all represented in training: this is seen-scanner evaluation on unseen specimens, not evidence of generalization to a new scanner. Each scanner panel contains only 16 scans from the same six validation specimens.

6 · Rigid-transform checks reveal dependence on pose

model variant original_BA transformed_BA changed_predictions

Rotating the unchanged sample by 90° around its surface axis reduces PointNeXt-S RGB from 98.6% to 87.5% balanced accuracy (7/64 predictions change) and Concerto RGB from 93.1% to 84.0% (8/64 change). This is a real robustness question even when original classification is strong. Test multiple rotations, point orders and sampling realizations. Compare pose augmentation and consistent alignment while preserving scanner-held-out assessment.

The translation check shifts normalized coordinates by (0.1, −0.1, 0.05), equivalent to (1, −1, 0.5) mm with scale_mm=10; it is not a 0.1 mm displacement. PointNeXt-S RGB falls to 95.8% and Concerto RGB to 92.4%. The 90° tests were not rerun from checkpoints in this review; these values come from the saved diagnostics.

7 · Existing focus maps do not explain the RGB winners

The archive has 48 occlusion maps: 12 examples for each geometry-only baseline, seed 42. All four consistency audits report exact agreement between saved and direct probabilities, and all show actual scanner RGB for context. The model itself received zero RGB in these runs, so apparent agreement between an overlay and stain colour is not evidence that it used colour.

The maps perturb 4×4 spatial regions by removing points and refilling the remaining cloud to fixed size. They explain sensitivity of the predicted class, which can be wrong, and change sampling density as well as local content. They are neither segmentation masks nor verified plaque-attribution maps. The strongest RGB runs have no focus export in this archive.

Generate maps for RGB PointNeXt-S and RGB Concerto and include their high-confidence errors. Use fixed examples across models, report the explained class and probability change, and compare to independent manual plaque masks when available.

8 · Inspect named scans before broad retraining

  • TRIOS5 BCG2T0-1: the only PointNeXt-S RGB error; review acquisition-stage metadata, raw colour and the corresponding three other scanners.
  • iTERO BCG4T2-5: clean classified partial by Concerto RGB with 99.8% confidence; iTERO BCG4T0-5 is also classified partial with 94.4% confidence. Review specimen-specific staining, material, residue, scan colour and stage definition; do not relabel from model confidence alone.
  • TRIOS5 BCG4T1-2: training Rq=0.188 mm and height range=1.337 mm, compared with development median Rq=0.00537 mm. Also inspect TRIOS5 BCG6T0-7 (Rq=0.135 mm). These may be geometric defects, crop/registration artifacts or real surface changes; raw inspection is required.
  • iTERO BCG4T1-5 and BCG5T0-8: validation roughness outliers, relevant when interpreting iTERO errors. Use an outcome-independent QC rule if exclusion becomes necessary, and retain results with/without exclusions.

9 · Prioritized investigation plan

Growth-group check: partial-stage examples exist only in G3–G6. On the mature-only validation subset, PointNeXt-S RGB seed 42 is correct on 48/48 scans and Concerto RGB on 43/48 (89.6% balanced accuracy), from only four physical specimens. Thus PointNeXt-S success is not confined to separating fresh from mature scans at evaluation. These models were still trained using all groups. A separately trained G3–G6-only experiment, with all three stages represented within the same group type, is needed to address the training confound.

  1. Separate colour statistics from spatial learning. Run the matched direct-statistics-only, encoder-only RGB and combined variants; add within-scan colour permutation and a 3D grayscale/intensity variant. Current 3D geometry-only removes all RGB, whereas the new 2D grayscale ablation retains intensity, so the two ablations answer different questions.
  2. Establish generalization using outer specimen folds and disjoint-subject scanner holdout. Include PointNeXt-S RGB, Concerto RGB, Sonata geometry and the colour/density controls. Keep reserved test untouched until the protocol is fixed. Important: the delivered 3D full-suite planner currently adds only area_geometry for the ablation-model list (PointNeXt-S and Concerto by default); simply running its default full suite will not assess the RGB winners or Sonata in those folds. Extend the plan deliberately.
  3. Test reconstruction and edge effects. Common-resolution remeshing, repeat surface sampling, an interior ROI, source-export audits, and phantom/repeat scans. Preserve physical units. On these exports median surface Rq is only about 5.4 μm, while the pretrained voxel grid is 0.1 mm in physical units; the grid does not imply all sub-grid detail is lost, but the physical feature scale and precision deserve explicit checks.
  4. Improve pose robustness and inspect errors. Add controlled rotations and sampling seeds; regenerate focus maps for RGB winners; review the named scans using original colour and geometry. Reassess scalar normalization and neighborhood scales before dismissing models that fail to learn geometry-only classes.
  5. Evaluate the actual segmentation/fusion target once labels arrive. Use manually annotated partial-stage regions and report area-weighted 3D Dice/IoU, sensitivity and boundary error. Compare 2D-only, geometry-only, colour-aware 3D-only and fused models on identical assessment specimens. A colour-aware 3D branch may duplicate the 2D branch; geometry must demonstrate incremental value rather than being assumed useful from the stage score.

10 · What can be said now

  • Supported: the current colour-aware PointNeXt-S configuration classifies the six validation specimens extremely well; colour is a strong source of stage information.
  • Supported: Sonata is the strongest repeated geometry-only baseline under the tested settings, and geometry-only performance varies materially with scanner and sampling.
  • Supported: mesh density is tightly associated with stage, and a scanner-plus-density control is competitive with the geometry models.
  • Not established: that PointNeXt-S is generally superior; that the 3D encoder is detecting biofilm topography; that predictions transfer to unseen scanners; that good stage classification implies good segmentation; or that 2D–3D fusion will improve performance.

Appendix · All 23 validation runs

BA and recall are percentages. The saved 95% intervals resample whole specimens within fresh/mature strata and are conditional on a fixed fitted model/split. They do not account for checkpoint selection, variant selection, retraining, future scanner domains or the small number of biological subjects. The narrow 97.2–100% interval for RGB PointNeXt-S should not be presented as a population-level guarantee.
